When someone calls a man or boy effeminate, they mean he has qualities, behaviors, or an appearance that are traditionally associated with women rather than men. Think of it as a word that says: "This male person seems more feminine than society typically expects a male person to be."

It is almost always applied to males. You would not describe a woman as effeminate, because that would make no sense — it would be like saying a woman seems "too womanly." The word only carries meaning when there is a contrast between the person's gender (male) and the qualities being observed (feminine).
What does it actually look like?

When people use this word, they are usually referring to things like a soft, high-pitched, or delicate voice; gentle or graceful body movements; a careful or dainty way of gesturing with the hands; a very polished or delicate physical appearance; or mannerisms and interests that society has traditionally labelled as belonging to women. None of these things are objectively "female-only" traits — they are simply traits that culture has, over a long time, decided to associate more with women than with men. The word effeminate is essentially pointing to that gap between expectation and observation.
The tone and feeling of the word

This is where the word gets layered and important to understand. Historically, effeminate was almost always used as a criticism or an insult toward men. The underlying assumption was that being masculine was the correct or desirable state for a man, and that having feminine qualities was a weakness, a flaw, or something shameful. Calling a man effeminate was a way of saying he was not "man enough."

Because of this history, the word carries a noticeably negative charge even today. It is not a neutral, scientific word. It is a loaded word — meaning it brings emotional weight and judgment along with it. When you read or hear it in older literature, historical texts, or formal writing, it often signals disapproval or condescension toward the person being described.

In modern, everyday usage, many people consider it offensive or at the very least old-fashioned, precisely because it treats femininity as something undesirable in a man. Using it can imply that being gentle, soft-spoken, or graceful is somehow beneath a male person — which is a value judgment, not a fact. So in contemporary conversation, you will find that many people avoid it or use it carefully, while others still use it casually or as a descriptive term without meaning to offend.

It is important not to confuse effeminate with related but different ideas.

It does not mean gay or homosexual. A man's mannerisms and appearance have nothing to do with his sexual orientation, and assuming otherwise is a stereotype. An effeminate man may be gay, straight, bisexual, or anything else — the word says nothing about who he is attracted to.

It does not mean weak in a physical sense, though historically it was often used that way.

It does not mean the person is pretending, performing, or acting in a calculated way. It simply describes how someone comes across in terms of manner and appearance.

It is also different from the word feminine. Feminine is a neutral descriptor that can apply to anyone or anything associated with womanhood, and it does not carry the same critical edge. Effeminate, by contrast, specifically implies an unexpected or unwanted degree of femininity in a male.

"His critics described his poetry as effeminate and soft, though his readers adored it for exactly those reasons."

"The new actor had an effeminate quality about him — a lightness in his step and a softness in his speech — that made him perfect for the role."

"In earlier centuries, men who showed emotion in public were often dismissed as effeminate."

In summary, effeminate is an adjective used to describe a male person whose manner, voice, appearance, or behavior resembles qualities that society traditionally associates with women. It has a long history of being used judgmentally — to suggest that such a man is falling short of masculine expectations. Today, it sits in contested territory: some use it plainly as a descriptive word, while others see it as carrying an outdated and unfair bias against femininity. Understanding both its meaning and its baggage is what makes you truly fluent in how this word works.
